exposure.uncertaintyBasis: Utility-scale renewable project WACCs in a large emerging market run 8-10% nominal in 2026 having fallen from 14-15% in 2010 as offtake contracts standardised, with higher-risk project categories at 10-12%; the band is set slightly wider at both ends to span the range between a strongly-rated upper-middle-income sovereign such as Chile and a weaker one. INDIA IS A PROXY, NOT CHILE: Chile is a stronger sovereign credit and would plausibly finance nearer the OECD band, so this row should be replaced with Chile-specific project-finance evidence before it drives a published figure.

Published 2026 cost-of-capital work for OECD energy infrastructure gives real WACCs of 6.5-7.5% for unregulated electricity and gas transmission and 7.0-7.5% for utility-scale solar and onshore wind, which at a 2% inflation assumption is roughly 8.5-9.6% nominal; a 2026 US midstream energy assessment gives 9.8% nominal. The band is set below those figures at its lower end because shipping assets are mobile, liquid collateral that supports cheaper senior debt than fixed energy infrastructure.

groups.label: Delivered energy demand
groups.rationale: Consumption scales with distance x roundtrips, and the two sides stay energy-matched via their LHV ratio. Perturbed together, so the corridor still delivers a physically consistent amount of energy.

exposure.uncertaintyBasis: London maritime arbitration customarily allows a margin of 0.5 knots on speed and 5% on fuel consumption where the warranty is qualified by 'about', which fixes the symmetric contractual tolerance; the upside is skewed because performance warranties apply only on good-weather days (Beaufort 4 / Douglas Sea State 3 or better) and therefore exclude heavy-weather passages and progressive hull fouling between dry-dockings, both of which raise realised annual consumption above the warranted figure.

London maritime arbitration customarily allows a margin of 0.5 knots on speed and 5% on fuel consumption where the warranty is qualified by 'about', which fixes the symmetric contractual tolerance; the upside is skewed because performance warranties apply only on good-weather days (Beaufort 4 / Douglas Sea State 3 or better) and therefore exclude heavy-weather passages and progressive hull fouling between dry-dockings, both of which raise realised annual consumption above the warranted figure.

Widened from the deep-sea range because a short-sea feeder spends a materially larger share of its annual energy in port, manoeuvring and pilotage - none of which falls inside the good-weather sea-passage envelope that the +/-5% charter-party tolerance describes. The widening is a judgement, not a measurement: no source quantifying the port-energy share of a 1,800 TEU feeder's annual consumption was found.

groups.label: Green delivered fuel cost
groups.rationale: Price x consumption is one quantity — the cost of delivered energy. Sweeping them apart double-counts the same exposure.

groups.label: Fossil delivered fuel cost
groups.rationale: As fuel-cost-green, on the incumbent side.

groups.label: Fleet capital
groups.rationale: Both sides are ordered from the same yard market, so a newbuild price shock moves them together; their SPREAD is the green premium and is a second axis, not this one. NOTE the researched caveat: over a 15-year horizon yard prices across CLASSES do not move together (Ultramax -27% and Kamsarmax -19% from 2007 to 2024 while the aggregate index moved 2.6%), so this group couples the two SIDES of one class, never two classes — see docs/corridor/input-uncertainty-findings.md.

exposure.unit: USD million per ship, conventional newbuild
exposure.uncertaintyBasis: Five reported 2026 Supramax/Ultramax newbuilding contracts span USD 33.5m to USD 39.2m, with the spread driven almost entirely by build country: Chinese yards cluster at USD 33.5-35m and the one Japanese order (Nihon Shipyard/Imabari) sits at USD 39.2m, a 17% premium for the same deadweight.

exposure.unit: USD million per ship, conventional newbuild
exposure.uncertaintyBasis: Reported 2026 Newcastlemax and large Capesize contracts cluster USD 73.5-78.25m, with a 2024 assessed value of USD 69.63m for 180,000 dwt setting the floor of the recent cycle; the model's current USD 80.5m point sits above every conventional contract found.

exposure.unit: USD million per ship, conventional newbuild
exposure.uncertaintyBasis: One reported 2026 feeder programme prices three 1,800 TEU vessels at USD 93-99m in total, i.e. USD 31-33m each, and the source itself expresses the figure as a range rather than a contract price; the band is widened modestly at both ends because this is a single datapoint.

groups.label: Fleet operating cost
groups.rationale: Same reasoning as fleet-capital: one hull class crewed, insured and maintained in one market, so an operating-cost move lifts both sides together. The disclosed peer spread that sizes this range is itself deadweight-normalised, which is why it measures management efficiency rather than class.

exposure.unit: USD million per ship per year, excluding fuel
exposure.uncertaintyBasis: Four listed dry bulk owners with similar average fleet deadweight disclosed daily operating expenses spanning USD 5,180 to USD 6,805 per vessel in Q2 2026 - a 31% cross-sectional spread between well-run public operators - to which a dry-dock accrual of roughly USD 450-800/day must be added, since the disclosed figures report dry docking separately.

exposure.unit: USD million per ship per year, excluding fuel
exposure.uncertaintyBasis: Same disclosed operator band as the Supramax row, shifted upward by a class premium of roughly 1.15-1.25x. Vessel operating cost scales far more weakly than deadweight because crew - about 42% of the total - is essentially flat between the classes (both carry some 20-22 seafarers, and minimum safe manning steps by gross tonnage are small). Only hull-and-machinery insurance (tracking a 2.2x hull value), lubricants (tracking engine power) and repairs scale materially, giving a weighted ratio near 1.24x against a deadweight ratio of 3.6x. No operator publishes opex split by class, so the premium is inferred from cost structure, not measured.

exposure.unit: USD million per ship per year, excluding fuel
exposure.uncertaintyBasis: No listed feeder container owner discloses technical operating cost separately: the largest pure feeder owner guides on USD 8,510 per vessel-day but that figure bundles voyage expenditure, G&A and ship management alongside OPEX, so it bounds the answer from above without giving it. The band is the dry bulk range widened at both ends.
